solution:
A motion is periodic only if it repeats itself at regular intervals of time.

(a) Not periodic. The swimmer makes one return trip only; the motion is to and fro but it is not repeated at regular intervals.

(b) Periodic. Released from a displaced position, the bar magnet oscillates about the N-S direction under the restoring torque of the earth's magnetic field, repeating its motion at regular intervals.

(c) Periodic. The molecule returns to the same configuration after each complete rotation about its centre of mass, so the motion repeats at regular intervals.

(d) Not periodic. The arrow travels once along its flight path and never returns to repeat it.

Periodic: (b) and (c). Not periodic: (a) and (d).

Simple harmonic motion is a to and fro motion about a mean position in which the restoring force is proportional to the displacement; other repetitive motions are periodic but not simple harmonic.

(a) Periodic but not simple harmonic. The earth spins steadily about its axis; there is no to and fro motion about a mean position and no restoring force.

(b) Simple harmonic. If the mercury level in one limb is displaced by \(y\), the level difference is \(2y\) and the unbalanced weight gives a restoring force proportional to \(y\).

(c) Simple harmonic. Released close to the lowest point, the ball bearing oscillates about that point with a restoring force proportional to the small displacement, exactly as for a simple pendulum of length equal to the radius of the bowl.

(d) Periodic but not simple harmonic. A polyatomic molecule has several independent normal modes, each simple harmonic but with its own frequency; the resultant vibration is a superposition of them and so is periodic without being simple harmonic.

Simple harmonic: (b) and (c). Periodic but not simple harmonic: (a) and (d).

[Textbook misprint in the figure caption: the question cites Fig. 13.18, and the figure attached above is the right one, but the book prints its caption as "Fig. 18.18" — a stray 8 for the chapter number. There is no Fig. 18.18; this chapter is 13.] A plot represents periodic motion only if the whole shape of the curve repeats itself after a fixed interval of time.

(a) Non-periodic. The displacement rises steadily and never returns to an earlier value.

(b) Periodic. The saw-tooth shape repeats itself exactly, and successive repetitions are \(2\,\text{s}\) apart, so the period is \(T = 2\,\text{s}\).

(c) Non-periodic. Although the curve rises and falls repeatedly, the successive humps differ in height and shape (the peak between \(t = 7\,\text{s}\) and \(t = 10\,\text{s}\) is much taller than the rest), so no complete shape is repeated.

(d) Periodic. The curve is sinusoidal and completes three full cycles between \(t = -3\,\text{s}\) and \(t = 3\,\text{s}\), so the period is \(T = 2\,\text{s}\).

Periodic: (b) with \(T = 2\,\text{s}\) and (d) with \(T = 2\,\text{s}\). Non-periodic: (a) and (c).

A function is simple harmonic only if it is a single sine or cosine of time; a sum of such terms with commensurate frequencies is periodic but not simple harmonic.

(a) \(\sin \omega t - \cos \omega t = \sqrt{2}\,\sin(\omega t - \pi/4)\). Simple harmonic, \(T = 2\pi/\omega\).

(b) \(\sin^3 \omega t = \dfrac{3\sin \omega t - \sin 3\omega t}{4}\). This is a sum of two simple harmonic terms of angular frequencies \(\omega\) and \(3\omega\), so it is periodic but not simple harmonic, with \(T = 2\pi/\omega\).

(c) \(3\cos(\pi/4 - 2\omega t) = 3\cos(2\omega t - \pi/4)\). Simple harmonic with angular frequency \(2\omega\), so \(T = 2\pi/2\omega = \pi/\omega\).

(d) \(\cos \omega t + \cos 3\omega t + \cos 5\omega t\). A sum of three simple harmonic terms whose angular frequencies are all multiples of \(\omega\); periodic but not simple harmonic, with \(T = 2\pi/\omega\).

(e) \(\exp(-\omega^2 t^2)\). Non-periodic. It falls off steadily on either side of \(t = 0\) and never repeats a value in a regular way.

(f) \(1 + \omega t + \omega^2 t^2\). Non-periodic. It increases without limit as \(t\) grows and never repeats.

Simple harmonic: (a) with \(T = 2\pi/\omega\) and (c) with \(T = \pi/\omega\). Periodic but not simple harmonic: (b) and (d), each with \(T = 2\pi/\omega\). Non-periodic: (e) and (f).

Take the mean position O at the mid-point of AB, so A is at \(x = -5\,\text{cm}\) and B is at \(x = +5\,\text{cm}\), with the direction A to B positive. In SHM the acceleration and the force are \(a = -\omega^2 x\) and \(F = -m\omega^2 x\), so both always point towards O, i.e. their sign is opposite to that of \(x\). The sign of the velocity is simply the direction of travel.

(a) At the end A the particle is momentarily at rest, and \(x\) is negative, so \(a\) and \(F\) point towards B. Velocity zero, acceleration positive, force positive.

(b) At the end B the particle is momentarily at rest, and \(x\) is positive. Velocity zero, acceleration negative, force negative.

(c) At the mid-point going towards A, \(x = 0\) so there is no restoring force, and the motion is towards A. Velocity negative, acceleration zero, force zero.

(d) At \(2\,\text{cm}\) from B towards A, \(x = +3\,\text{cm}\) and the motion is towards A. Velocity negative, acceleration negative, force negative.

(e) At \(3\,\text{cm}\) from A towards B, \(x = -2\,\text{cm}\) and the motion is towards B. Velocity positive, acceleration positive, force positive.

(f) At \(4\,\text{cm}\) from B towards A, \(x = +1\,\text{cm}\) and the motion is towards A. Velocity negative, acceleration negative, force negative.

Signs of (velocity, acceleration, force): (a) \(0, +, +\); (b) \(0, -, -\); (c) \(-, 0, 0\); (d) \(-, -, -\); (e) \(+, +, +\); (f) \(-, -, -\).

A motion is simple harmonic only when the acceleration is proportional to the displacement AND directed opposite to it, i.e. \(a = -\omega^2 x\) with \(\omega^2\) a positive constant.

Testing each relation: \(a = 0.7x\) is proportional to \(x\) but has the same sign as \(x\), so the force pushes the particle away from the mean position and the motion is not oscillatory. \(a = -200x^2\) is not proportional to \(x\), and being always negative it does not reverse as \(x\) reverses. \(a = 100x^3\) is neither proportional to \(x\) nor oppositely directed.

Only \(a = -10x\) has the required form, with \(\omega^2 = 10\,\text{s}^{-2}\), i.e. \(\omega = \sqrt{10}\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\).

The relation \(a = -10x\) represents simple harmonic motion.

For \(x(t) = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)\), the velocity is \(v(t) = -A\omega\sin(\omega t + \phi)\).

At \(t = 0\), \(x_0 = A\cos\phi = 1\,\text{cm}\) and \(v_0 = -A\omega\sin\phi = \omega\,\text{cm s}^{-1}\), so \(A\sin\phi = -1\,\text{cm}\).

Squaring and adding, \(A^2 = (1)^2 + (-1)^2 = 2\), so \(A = \sqrt{2}\,\text{cm} \approx 1.414\,\text{cm}\).

Dividing, \(\tan\phi = -1\). Since \(\cos\phi\) is positive and \(\sin\phi\) is negative, \(\phi\) lies in the fourth quadrant:

\(\phi = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) (equivalently \(\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\), or \(315^\circ\)).

For the sine form \(x = B\sin(\omega t + \alpha)\), the velocity is \(v = B\omega\cos(\omega t + \alpha)\). At \(t = 0\), \(B\sin\alpha = 1\,\text{cm}\) and \(B\omega\cos\alpha = \omega\,\text{cm s}^{-1}\), so \(B\cos\alpha = 1\,\text{cm}\).

Hence \(B^2 = 1 + 1 = 2\), giving \(B = \sqrt{2}\,\text{cm}\), and \(\tan\alpha = 1\) with both \(\sin\alpha\) and \(\cos\alpha\) positive, so \(\alpha = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) \((45^\circ)\).

The value \(\omega = \pi\,\text{s}^{-1}\) is not needed, because it cancels out of the velocity condition.

Cosine form: amplitude \(\sqrt{2}\,\text{cm}\), initial phase \(-\pi/4\). Sine form: amplitude \(\sqrt{2}\,\text{cm}\), initial phase \(\pi/4\).

First find the spring constant from the scale. The full scale reading corresponds to a load of \(50\,\text{kg}\), whose weight is

\(F = mg = 50\,\text{kg} \times 9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2} = 490\,\text{N}\),

and this stretches the spring through the whole scale length \(x = 20\,\text{cm} = 0.20\,\text{m}\). Hence

\(k = \dfrac{F}{x} = \dfrac{490\,\text{N}}{0.20\,\text{m}} = 2450\,\text{N m}^{-1}\).

For a mass \(m\) suspended from this spring, \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}\), so

\(m = \dfrac{kT^2}{4\pi^2} = \dfrac{2450\,\text{N m}^{-1} \times (0.6\,\text{s})^2}{4\pi^2} = \dfrac{882}{39.48}\,\text{kg} = 22.3\,\text{kg}\).

The weight of the body is

\(W = mg = 22.3\,\text{kg} \times 9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2} = 219\,\text{N}\).

The body has a mass of about \(22.3\,\text{kg}\) and a weight of about \(219\,\text{N}\).

The mass on the spring executes SHM with angular frequency

\(\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1200\,\text{N m}^{-1}}{3\,\text{kg}}} = \sqrt{400}\,\text{rad s}^{-1} = 20\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\).

The mass is released from rest \(2.0\,\text{cm}\) from the equilibrium position, so the amplitude is \(A = 2.0\,\text{cm} = 0.02\,\text{m}\).

(i) Frequency: \(\nu = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi} = \dfrac{20}{2\pi}\,\text{Hz} = 3.2\,\text{Hz}\).

(ii) Maximum acceleration: \(a_{\max} = \omega^2 A = (20\,\text{rad s}^{-1})^2 \times 0.02\,\text{m} = 8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), occurring at the extreme positions.

(iii) Maximum speed: \(v_{\max} = \omega A = 20\,\text{rad s}^{-1} \times 0.02\,\text{m} = 0.4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), occurring at the mean position.

(i) \(3.2\,\text{Hz}\); (ii) \(8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\); (iii) \(0.4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

From Exercise 13.9 the amplitude is \(A = 2\,\text{cm}\) and the angular frequency is \(\omega = 20\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\), so in every case \(x\) is measured in cm and \(t\) in s.

(a) At the mean position at \(t = 0\), the displacement must be zero at \(t = 0\) and then grow in the positive direction:

\(x = 2\sin 20t\)

(b) At the maximum stretched position at \(t = 0\), the displacement is \(+A\) at \(t = 0\):

\(x = 2\cos 20t\)

(c) At the maximum compressed position at \(t = 0\), the displacement is \(-A\) at \(t = 0\):

\(x = -2\cos 20t\)

Written in the common form \(x = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)\), these are \(2\cos(20t - \pi/2)\), \(2\cos(20t)\) and \(2\cos(20t + \pi)\).

All three functions have the same amplitude \(2\,\text{cm}\) and the same angular frequency \(20\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\); they differ only in the initial phase, which is \(-\pi/2\), \(0\) and \(\pi\) respectively.

[Textbook answer-key error (part b, unit only): the printed key gives the correct function and coefficient but adds "where \(x\) is in cm". Fig. 13.20(b) labels that circle \(2\,\text{m}\), and the radius of the reference circle IS the amplitude, so \(x\) is in metres. The book uses each unit correctly elsewhere in the very same figure — panel (a) is labelled \(3\,\text{cm}\) — so this is a slip on (b)'s line, not a convention carried across. Part (a) agrees with the key exactly.] If the reference particle starts at an angle \(\phi_0\) to the positive \(x\)-axis, then for anticlockwise revolution its angle at time \(t\) is \(\phi_0 + \omega t\) and for clockwise revolution it is \(\phi_0 - \omega t\). The \(x\)-projection is the radius times the cosine of that angle.

(a) Here the radius is \(3\,\text{cm}\), \(T = 2\,\text{s}\) so \(\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} = \pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\), P starts at the lowest point of the circle so \(\phi_0 = -\pi/2\), and the revolution is clockwise. Therefore

\(x(t) = 3\cos\!\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \pi t\right) = 3\cos\!\left(\pi t + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = -3\sin(\pi t)\;\text{cm}\)

(b) Here the radius is \(2\,\text{m}\), \(T = 4\,\text{s}\) so \(\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{4} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\), P starts on the negative \(x\)-axis so \(\phi_0 = \pi\), and the revolution is anticlockwise. Therefore

\(x(t) = 2\cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}t + \pi\right) = -2\cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{2}\right)\;\text{m}\)

Since P starts on the \(x\)-axis in this case, the same expression is obtained whichever sense of revolution is taken.

(a) \(x(t) = -3\sin(\pi t)\,\text{cm}\); (b) \(x(t) = -2\cos(\pi t/2)\,\text{m}\).

Write each motion in the standard form \(x = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)\). The reference circle then has radius \(A\), the rotating particle has angular speed \(\omega\) (anticlockwise), and at \(t = 0\) it sits at the angle \(\phi\) measured from the positive \(x\)-axis.

(a) \(x = -2\sin(3t + \pi/3) = 2\cos\!\left(3t + \dfrac{\pi}{3} + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 2\cos\!\left(3t + \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)\).

Radius \(2\,\text{cm}\), angular speed \(3\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\), initial position at \(150^\circ\) from the positive \(x\)-axis (so \(x = -\sqrt{3}\,\text{cm}\) at \(t = 0\)).

(b) \(x = \cos(\pi/6 - t) = \cos\!\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\), since the cosine is an even function.

Radius \(1\,\text{cm}\), angular speed \(1\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\), initial position at \(-30^\circ\) from the positive \(x\)-axis.

(c) \(x = 3\sin(2\pi t + \pi/4) = 3\cos\!\left(2\pi t + \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 3\cos\!\left(2\pi t - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\).

Radius \(3\,\text{cm}\), angular speed \(2\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\), initial position at \(-45^\circ\) from the positive \(x\)-axis.

(d) \(x = 2\cos \pi t\) is already in standard form.

Radius \(2\,\text{cm}\), angular speed \(\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\), initial position on the positive \(x\)-axis \((\phi = 0)\).

In each case the required plot is a circle of the stated radius centred on the origin, with P marked at the stated angle and an anticlockwise arrow labelled with the stated angular speed.

(a) In Fig. 13.21(a) the wall supplies an equal and opposite reaction, so the spring is stretched by the force \(\mathbf{F}\) acting at its free end. At maximum extension the spring force balances the applied force, \(kx = F\), giving

\(x = \dfrac{F}{k}\)

In Fig. 13.21(b) the two applied forces are equal and opposite, so the spring as a whole is in equilibrium and the tension in it is again \(F\) throughout. Hence the maximum extension is again

\(x = \dfrac{F}{k}\)

The maximum extension is \(F/k\) in both cases.

(b) In Fig. 13.21(a) a single mass \(m\) oscillates on a spring whose other end is fixed, so

\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}\)

In Fig. 13.21(b) both masses move. The centre of the spring stays at rest, so each mass behaves as though attached to a spring of half the length, whose force constant is \(2k\); equivalently the system oscillates with the reduced mass \(\mu = \dfrac{m \times m}{m + m} = \dfrac{m}{2}\). Either way

\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{\mu}{k}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{2k}}\)

Periods: \(2\pi\sqrt{m/k}\) for Fig. 13.21(a) and \(2\pi\sqrt{m/2k}\) for Fig. 13.21(b).

The stroke is twice the amplitude, so

\(A = \dfrac{1.0\,\text{m}}{2} = 0.5\,\text{m}\).

The angular frequency is \(\omega = 200\,\text{rad min}^{-1}\). The maximum speed of a particle in SHM is

\(v_{\max} = \omega A = 200\,\text{rad min}^{-1} \times 0.5\,\text{m} = 100\,\text{m min}^{-1}\).

Converting to SI,

\(v_{\max} = \dfrac{100\,\text{m}}{60\,\text{s}} = 1.67\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

The maximum speed of the piston is \(100\,\text{m min}^{-1} = 1.67\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

The period of a simple pendulum is \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}\). The length \(L\) is unchanged, so \(T \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{g}}\) and

\(\dfrac{T_m}{T_e} = \sqrt{\dfrac{g_e}{g_m}}\)

where the subscripts \(m\) and \(e\) denote the moon and the earth. Substituting \(T_e = 3.5\,\text{s}\), \(g_e = 9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) and \(g_m = 1.7\,\text{m s}^{-2}\),

\(T_m = 3.5\,\text{s} \times \sqrt{\dfrac{9.8}{1.7}} = 3.5\,\text{s} \times \sqrt{5.76} = 3.5 \times 2.40\,\text{s}\)

\(T_m = 8.4\,\text{s}\)

The time period on the surface of the moon is about \(8.4\,\text{s}\).

[Textbook inconsistency in the printed hint: the key's formula is correct and the answer below matches it character for character, but the hint printed alongside it says the effective acceleration due to gravity "will get reduced" by the radial acceleration. The key's own formula has \(g_{\text{eff}} = \sqrt{g^{2} + (v^{2}/R)^{2}}\), which is GREATER than \(g\) — the two accelerations are perpendicular, so they add in quadrature and the effective value increases. The key refutes its own hint; the formula is the half to trust.] In the frame of the car the bob is acted on by two accelerations at right angles to each other: the acceleration due to gravity \(g\), vertically downwards, and the centripetal acceleration \(\dfrac{v^2}{R}\), directed horizontally towards the centre of the circular track.

The bob therefore hangs along the resultant of these, and the effective acceleration governing small oscillations is their vector sum

\(g_{\text{eff}} = \sqrt{g^2 + \left(\dfrac{v^2}{R}\right)^2}\)

Small oscillations about this new equilibrium direction are simple harmonic with the usual pendulum formula, but with \(g\) replaced by \(g_{\text{eff}}\):

\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g_{\text{eff}}}}\)

\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{\sqrt{g^2 + \dfrac{v^4}{R^2}}}}\)

The mass \(M\) of the bob does not enter the result.

Let \(\rho\) be the density of the cork, \(\rho_l\) the density of the liquid, \(A\) the base area and \(h\) the height of the cork.

Floating in equilibrium, the weight of the cork is balanced by the buoyant force on the submerged part. Now let the cork be pushed down through a small further distance \(x\) and released. An extra volume \(Ax\) of liquid is displaced, so there is an extra upward buoyant force

\(F = -A x \rho_l g\)

the negative sign showing that it acts opposite to the displacement, i.e. it is a restoring force proportional to \(x\). The motion is therefore simple harmonic.

The mass of the cork is \(m = A h \rho\), so the acceleration is

\(a = \dfrac{F}{m} = -\dfrac{A \rho_l g}{A h \rho}\,x = -\dfrac{\rho_l g}{h \rho}\,x\)

Comparing with \(a = -\omega^2 x\),

\(\omega^2 = \dfrac{\rho_l g}{h \rho}\), so \(\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{\rho_l g}{h \rho}}\)

and hence

\(T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{h\rho}{\rho_l g}}\)

which is the required result.

Let \(A\) be the cross-sectional area of the tube, \(\rho\) the density of mercury and \(L\) the total length of the mercury column.

While the suction pump maintains the pressure difference, the mercury stands lower in one limb than in the other. When the pump is removed, suppose the level in one limb is a distance \(y\) below its equilibrium level; then the level in the other limb is \(y\) above its own equilibrium level, so the difference in the two mercury levels is \(2y\).

The weight of this unbalanced column of height \(2y\) is the restoring force:

\(F = -(2y)A\rho g\)

the negative sign showing that it acts so as to reduce \(y\). The force is proportional to the displacement and directed towards the equilibrium position, so the motion is simple harmonic.

The mass of mercury set in motion is \(m = L A \rho\), so

\(a = \dfrac{F}{m} = -\dfrac{2 A \rho g}{L A \rho}\,y = -\dfrac{2g}{L}\,y\)

Comparing with \(a = -\omega^2 y\) gives \(\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{2g}{L}}\), and hence the mercury column oscillates simple harmonically with period

\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{2g}}\)
